posts.on_image: YOU'RE NOT FULL. YOU'RE JUST TIRED OF CHEWING.
posts.caption: Grandma Ruth didn't believe in the word full. At Thanksgiving she walked the table with a serving spoon like a deputy on patrol, and if your plate showed any white, she fixed it. You could say no thank you, you could put your hand over the plate, it didn't matter. She'd just wait until you looked away. My cousin Donnie tried leaving a little on his plate as a signal, which only told her he liked it. By pie time we were all lying on her living room carpet in our church clothes, and she'd come in with a dish of mints in case anybody had room.
posts.first:
My grandmother fed us like a famine was coming Tuesday. She lived through the Depression on a farm outside Decatur, and an empty plate in her house was something you fixed, not something you admired. I loosened my belt one notch every Thanksgiving until I was about twenty-five.

posts.topic: standing on a chair while Mom pinned the hem
posts.on_image: SEWING THE DRESS: ONE WEEKEND / HOLDING STILL FOR THE HEM: FOREVER
posts.caption: Mom made most of my school dresses on a Singer at the kitchen table, and the sewing part went fast. She'd cut the pattern out on Friday night with the tissue pinned to the fabric and have the thing sewn by Sunday supper. Then came the hem. I stood on a kitchen chair while she crawled around my knees with a mouthful of straight pins, saying turn, turn, stop, hold still. If I so much as looked at the window, she'd mumble through those pins that I was going to get it crooked. I never argued, because I was too scared she'd swallow one. That blue dress lasted me two school years, since she'd folded three extra inches up inside the hem for later.
posts.first:
My mother could talk perfectly clear with six pins in her mouth, which I always thought was the most impressive thing she did. She wore a tomato pincushion on her wrist like a watch. I still can't stand on a chair without wanting to turn slowly to the left.

posts.topic: the fused ribbon candy in the good dish
posts.on_image: THE RIBBON CANDY IN THE GOOD DISH HAD BEEN ONE SOLID PIECE SINCE 1971.
posts.caption: Aunt Hazel kept a cut-glass dish of ribbon candy on the end table by her davenport, and as far as anybody could tell, it was the same candy every Christmas. It came out of the cedar chest in December with the nativity set and went back in January, dish and all. Somewhere along the way every piece had fused into one clump, so if you wanted some, you had to lift the whole thing out and knock a corner off against the glass. My brother Mike chipped a tooth on it in 1974 and still says it was worth it. Nobody ever saw Aunt Hazel eat a piece. I'm fairly sure it was there to be looked at, like the plastic grapes on her dining table.
posts.first:
Ours had a fine layer of dust on top that told you exactly how long it had been since anybody tried. When they cleaned out Aunt Hazel's house in 1983, three of us cousins wanted that candy dish more than anything else in the place. My sister Carol got it, and the candy is still in it.

posts.topic: Dad listening to the engine with the hood up
posts.on_image: EVERYBODY HUSH. I'M LISTENING TO THE ENGINE.
posts.caption: Every few weeks Dad decided the Plymouth was making a noise. Nobody else could hear it, but that didn't matter, because once he popped the hood the whole family was part of the investigation. Mom had to stop the washer. We had to stop bouncing the ball. Even the dog seemed to know to hold still while Dad leaned in with his head cocked, waiting for a tick only he could hear. Sometimes he'd tighten something with a dime from his pocket and announce it was fixed. The car sounded exactly the same to me, but it ran another nine years, so who am I to say.
posts.first:
My father could diagnose a car by sound from the other end of the house, or at least he said he could. He'd stop in the middle of supper, tilt his head, and say, "That's the fan belt." Half the time it was the neighbor's car.

posts.on_image: 212 VACATION SLIDES. / THREE WERE UPSIDE DOWN. DAD SHOWED THEM ANYWAY.
posts.caption: We took one trip west in the summer of '68, and Dad spent the next ten years showing it to us. Any time company came over, out came the screen on its wobbly tripod and the projector with the round tray that clacked every time it turned. He narrated each slide like a tour guide. That's the Grand Canyon. That's the Grand Canyon from the other side. That one's upside down, but you get the idea. Uncle Walt would be snoring by Arizona, and Dad kept right on going to the end of the tray.
posts.first:
We still have Dad's slides in four shoeboxes in my closet, labeled in his handwriting. I had a few made into prints a while back and found two more that were upside down. I left them that way.
